publicTrace: Base rate reference class: post-expanded-CTC SPM child poverty series (2022–2024). The 2022 rate was 12.4%, 2023 was 13.7%, and 2024 was 13.4%, giving a post-expansion average of approximately 13.2% and a recent one-year change of −0.3 pp. This three-year window is the primary reference class for 2025.

Point estimate mechanism: a weighted blend of the PolicyEngine current-law prior (13.0%, weight 0.55), the post-expansion historical average (13.2%, weight 0.35), and the latest published 2024 rate (13.4%, weight 0.10), minus a small macro adjustment of −0.05 pp, yields a calibrated point estimate of approximately 13.0%. The PolicyEngine input confirms no major current-law policy changes between 2024 and 2025 that would shift the rate substantially.

Upside risk (rate rises above 14.3%): SNAP benefit cliffs, expiration of pandemic-era transfer residuals, rising medical out-of-pocket costs, or a labor market softening in 2025 could push the SPM child poverty rate above the upper CI. Immigration enforcement disruptions to household income could also raise the rate.

Downside risk (rate falls below 11.9%): Stronger-than-expected EITC and CTC refund uptake, real wage growth concentrated among lower-income families with children, or favorable housing cost adjustments in SPM thresholds could push the rate below the lower CI.

Calibration note: the CDF is centered near 12.7% (median) with the point estimate at 13.0%, reflecting slight right-skew given that the 2023 spike to 13.7% demonstrated upside volatility. The 80% interval spans approximately 11.5% to 14.6%, consistent with the prototype calibration prior of ±1.1/1.3 pp half-widths around the point estimate, widened modestly because the PolicyEngine input is a stored prior rather than a fresh microsimulation run.

Data path qualification: the Census SPM tables page and release schedule were fetched successfully (HTTP 200), confirming the September 2026 release target. However, the child poverty history is a prototype seed and the PolicyEngine check is a stored prior, not a live microsimulation. Uncertainty is widened accordingly relative to a fully data-complete forecast.

Disconfirming scenario: if Congress enacted or extended refundable CTC provisions in late 2024 or early 2025 that took effect for tax year 2025, the rate could fall materially below 12%, outside our 80% interval. Conversely, a recession beginning in 2025 with significant job losses among parents of young children could push the rate above 15%.
assumptions: PolicyEngine current-law policy (ID 2, v0.654.1) reflects no major new child-poverty-relevant legislation enacted between the 2024 and 2025 tax years; any enacted changes would shift the distribution.
The post-expansion SPM child poverty series (2022–2024) is the appropriate reference class; pre-2022 rates are excluded because the expanded CTC and pandemic transfers created a structural break.
ASEC sampling error for the SPM child poverty rate is approximately ±0.3–0.5 pp at one standard error, contributing to the CI width alongside policy and price uncertainty.
No major methodological revision to SPM thresholds or resource definitions is assumed for the 2025 reference year; Census has periodically revised SPM methodology, which could shift the series.
Real household income growth and transfer program participation rates in 2025 are assumed to be broadly consistent with 2024 trends, absent a recession or major policy shock.
dataCaveats: The SPM child poverty history (2022–2024 rates of 12.4%, 13.7%, 13.4%) is a prototype seed value, not a machine-readable Census API pull; the actual published series may differ slightly.
The PolicyEngine prior of 13.0% is a stored estimate, not a fresh server-side microsimulation for calendar year 2025; a live run could yield a different central estimate.
SPM includes medical out-of-pocket expenses and geographic housing adjustments that can move the series independently of income or transfer policy, adding volatility not captured in the policy prior.
The Census release is scheduled for September 2026; any delay or methodological revision announcement before release would affect the forecast but is not modeled here.
Immigration enforcement actions in 2025 could affect household composition and income reporting in the ASEC in ways not captured by current-law microsimulation models.
drivers: EITC and CTC refund amounts and uptake rates among families with children
SNAP and Medicaid participation and benefit levels affecting SPM resource counts
Medical out-of-pocket expense trends affecting SPM resource deductions
Labor market conditions and wage growth for lower-income parents in 2025
Geographic housing cost adjustments embedded in SPM thresholds
